differences.aspect: Fit to the brief's core concept
differences.design_x: Design X option 1 is a direct race through a neon sci-fi city course with 7 ordered checkpoints, two lanes, and a finish portal; the prototype and build plan keep that same runner structure.
differences.design_y: Design Y option 1 is also a direct race through a neon sci-fi city course, with 9 ordered checkpoints, two long lanes, and a finish portal; the later steps preserve that same concept.
differences.evidence: Both sessions recommend option 1 and keep a walking race through a neon sci-fi course. Design X prototype: 'แข่งเดินเร็วผ่านเมืองไซไฟเรืองแสง เก็บ 7 เช็กพอยต์ หลบกระแสไฟ และเข้าโพรทัลให้เร็วกว่าเพื่อน' (race-walk through a glowing neon sci-fi city, collect 7 checkpoints, dodge electric hazards, enter the portal before friends). Design Y prototype: 'เกมเส้นทางเดินแข่งขันธีมนีออนไซไฟ ปรับจังหวะเป็นเดินเร็วเพื่อความปลอดภัย' (a neon sci-fi walking-race game adjusted to fast walking for safety).

differences.design_x: Design X is clear and coherent, but its build brief stays at the level of route shape, named beats, and broad placement guidance.
differences.design_y: Design Y gives more buildable detail: exact checkpoint labels, approximate spacing, hazard density progression, door clearance, spawn sightlines, and a more explicit spectator-facing finish.
differences.evidence: In the final build plan, Design X says to use 'a long two-lane-style zigzag route' with 'exactly 7 ordered checkpoints' and hazards 'at least 0.6 m from the play-area edge'. Design Y specifies 'exactly 9 ordered checkpoints, spaced approximately 2.5–9 m apart', names all 9 checkpoint labels, says the four real doors must remain completely clear, and describes hazard placement between specific checkpoint ranges (1–2, 4–6, 8–9).

differences.design_x: Design X addresses safety with wide lanes, no running, and hazard offsets, but it is less explicit about the venue's real doors and player separation details.
differences.design_y: Design Y is more operationally safety-conscious: it repeatedly calls out lane separation, no lane-cutting, door clearance, spawn separation, and avoiding tasks that make players look up while moving.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype decisions include 'เดินเร็วอย่างปลอดภัย ไม่วิ่งจริง' (walk fast safely, no real running), 'เว้นทาง 1.2 เมตร' (leave 1.2 m path width), and hazards at least 0.6 m from edges. Design Y goes further in the prototype and build plan: 'แยกจุดเริ่ม 6 คน ห้ามตัดเลนหรือวิ่ง' (separate starts for 6 players, no lane cutting or running), 'ไม่วางอะไรบนประตูทั้ง 4 บาน' (do not place anything on the four doors), and 'ไม่มีภารกิจที่ต้องเงยหน้าขณะเดินเร็ว' (no tasks requiring looking up while moving fast).

differences.design_x: Design X has a clean, simple race arc and is easy to understand, but its middle section is more generic: checkpoints, hazards, then finish.
differences.design_y: Design Y has a more shaped player experience with a teach-in, a mid-race twist, a calm beat, and a climax, which better supports a 5-minute session.
differences.evidence: Design X flow: 0:30 learn gates and red rings, 1:30 collect core and cross connection, 3:00 charge gate and final route, 4:15 head to city core. Design Y flow adds a clearer difficulty curve: 0:15 checkpoints 1–2 teach dodging, 1:15 checkpoint 3 story twist, 2:00 checkpoints 4–6 denser hazards, 3:15 checkpoint 7 calm scenic pause, 3:45 checkpoints 8–9 climax bridge. That is a more deliberate pacing design.

differences.design_x: Design X includes spectators and orients key moments toward them, but the plan is comparatively general.
differences.design_y: Design Y designs more explicitly for the family audience by placing the climax and finish near the long spectator side and tying the leaderboard wall screen into the experience.
differences.evidence: Design X spectator plan says families stand along the long side to see the mid-route dodge and final portal approach and follow the live leaderboard. Design Y build plan says the final two hazard groups, checkpoint 9, and the finish portal are placed near the long spectator side, and the prototype storyboard ends with the leaderboard visible to friends and family together.

differences.design_x: Design X stays consistent from option 1 to prototype to build plan: same title, same 7-checkpoint race, same scoring, same safety posture, same spectator framing.
differences.design_y: Design Y also stays internally consistent across all three steps: same title, same 9-checkpoint structure, same scoring, same safety constraints, same spectator emphasis.
differences.evidence: For Design X, option 1 already names 7 checkpoints, two lanes, 6 players, 5 minutes; the prototype and build plan repeat those details. For Design Y, option 1 names 9 checkpoints, two lanes, 6 players, 5 minutes; the prototype and build plan repeat those details and even preserve the same scoring rules (100 per checkpoint, -25 hazard penalty, 300 finish plus time bonus).

improvements: For Design X: add more concrete build constraints such as exact checkpoint spacing, door clearance, and hazard density by segment so the layout team has less ambiguity.
For Design X: consider adding a clearer mid-run pacing beat or scenic pause so the 5-minute race has more texture than a steady sequence of hazards.
For Design Y: simplify the course slightly if needed; 9 checkpoints in 5 minutes may feel busy for some players, especially with denser late hazards.
For Design Y: watch crowding risk from six separated spawns and strict lane discipline; a quick staff briefing or visual spawn markers may be needed in practice.
For both: include an explicit fallback for slower players so they still get a satisfying finish even if they are far behind near the time limit.
summary: Both designs fit the brief well and stay consistent from options to prototype to build plan. Design X is a clean, straightforward neon race with solid safety rules and a simple 7-checkpoint structure. Design Y is stronger overall because it is more specific, more safety-aware in the real venue, and better paced for a 5-minute group race, while also giving spectators a clearer show.
why: Design Y wins on the aspects that most affect the creator and players: build specificity, real-space safety, and pacing. It gives the builder exact checkpoint labels, spacing ranges, door-clearance rules, and a hazard progression that is easier to implement and test. It also designs the 5-minute session more deliberately, with an onboarding stretch, a mid-race escalation, a short recovery beat, and a climax near the spectators. Design X is still a good answer to the brief, but it is more generic in its middle game and less explicit about venue-specific safety details.
x_weaknesses: Less specific build guidance than Design Y, especially around exact spacing, door clearance, and hazard density by segment.
The race structure is simpler and a bit more generic, with fewer distinct pacing beats across the 5 minutes.
Spectator staging is good but less precisely designed than Design Y's finish-near-the-crowd approach.
y_weaknesses: The 9-checkpoint structure may be a little busier for a 5-minute race, especially for players who need time to read hazards.
The design depends on disciplined lane separation and spawn management; if that fails in practice, the experience could feel crowded.
The added narrative beats and scenic pause are strong, but they create slightly more production complexity than Design X.
